title: How Do You Plant a Church That Survives?
subtitle: Counting the cost before you break ground, surviving the first eighteen months, and knowing the difference between a crowd and a church

sections.title: Sit Down First and Count
sections.body:
Jesus said it about a tower and it has never been more about anything than it is about this. Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, to see whether he has enough to finish it. He said it as a warning, and church planters are among the people most likely to ignore the warning, because we are dreamers, and dreamers do not like to sit down and count.

So count. Count the money, honestly, including the eighteen months when there will be almost no money coming in and rent going out. Count the marriage, because planting will ask of your spouse a thing no one warned them about, years of instability with a smile required on Sundays. Count your own soul, because the same drive that makes you want to start something is the drive most likely to burn you to the ground when the something is slow to start.

Most plants that fail do not fail from bad theology or bad preaching. They fail from a cost that was never counted, a runway that was always too short, a planter who measured the dream and never measured the price. Count it now, on paper, with people who love you and will tell you the truth, before you tell anyone you are doing this. The counting is not a lack of faith. The counting is the form faith takes in a man who intends to finish.

sections.title: The First Eighteen Months Will Try You
sections.body:
There is a season after the excitement and before the stability that no one describes to you, and it is the season most plants die in. The launch team that was forty is now twenty two. The couple you were sure would be elders moved away for a job. The growth you projected on the spreadsheet has not arrived, and the spreadsheet is in your desk drawer accusing you every morning.

This is the valley, and the valley is normal, and the planters who quit in it almost always quit because they thought it meant something was wrong. It does not mean something is wrong. It means you are eighteen months into the hardest thing in ministry and the early enthusiasm has worn off and now only the call is left to carry you, and the call, it turns out, is enough, but only barely, and only if you stay.

Do not measure these months by attendance, because attendance in the first year and a half is the cruelest possible metric, swinging wildly on the weather and the holidays and whether the one big family was out of town. Measure them by faithfulness. Did you preach the Word. Did you love the few. Did you stay married, stay sane, stay on your knees. Those are the things that build a church under the surface long before the surface shows it. The numbers come or they do not, but the foundation is poured in the dark, in the valley, in the months no one will ever thank you for surviving.

sections.title: A Launch Is Not a Church
sections.body:
We have built a whole industry around the launch, the big Sunday, the marketing, the bounce houses and the mailers and the crowd of two hundred curious neighbors who came to see what the new thing was. And the launch is fine. But the launch is not a church, and confusing the two has ruined more planters than laziness ever did.

A crowd gathers around novelty. A church gathers around a cross. The two hundred who came to your launch came for many reasons, and most of those reasons will not survive contact with an ordinary rainy Sunday in February when the bounce house is gone and what remains is a man preaching repentance to people on folding chairs. The launch tests your marketing. The eighteenth month tests your church.

A church is not an event you produce. It is a body you cultivate, a people who are being knit to Christ and to one another so that they would still be a church if the lights failed and the band quit and the building flooded. The hard, unglamorous question is not how many came to the launch. It is how many are left, formed, committed, ready to suffer for one another, when the crowd has thinned to the people who actually mean it. Build for those people. They are the church. The crowd was only ever the soil they grew in.

sections.title: The Plant Will Hunt Your Identity
sections.body:
Here is the danger no demographic study will warn you about. The church you plant will become, if you are not careful, the place you go to find out whether you are worth anything, and that is a place no church can survive being.

The planter's ego and the planter's plant grow up tangled together. When attendance rises he feels like a man. When it falls he feels like a fraud. He cannot tell, most days, whether he wants the church to grow for the kingdom or for the proof, and the honest answer is usually both, and the both is what will destroy him, because a man who needs the church to succeed in order to feel loved will manipulate it, exhaust it, and finally resent it for failing to do a job it was never meant to do.

Your identity has to be settled before the plant, not by it. You are loved by God in Christ before the first Sunday and you will be loved by him just the same if the doors close in year three. Until that is bone deep in you, the plant will become an idol, and the idol will eat you, and it will do it while everyone praises your passion. Settle the question before you start. Then you can plant freely, because you will have nothing to prove, and a man with nothing to prove is the only kind of man who can lead a church without bleeding it for his own assurance.

sections.title: Plant What You Are Willing to Leave
sections.body:
The strange test of a healthy plant is whether it could survive you. The church built entirely on the planter's gifts is not a church. It is a platform, and when the planter leaves, the platform folds, because nothing was ever built that did not run through one man.

From the first eighteen months, build something you could one day walk away from without it collapsing. Raise leaders who are not you. Plant the gospel deeper than your personality, into the people themselves, so that the church is anchored to Christ and not to your charisma. This is the hardest discipline for a founder, because everything in you wants to be needed, and a church that does not need you feels like a church that does not love you. It is the opposite. It is the church you loved well enough to make free.

Count the cost. Survive the valley. Build a church and not a crowd. Settle your soul before you break ground. And then, having given it everything, hold it with an open hand, because it was never yours, and the proof that you planted well is the day it could go on without you.

The field is not the farmer's. He only works it. The harvest belongs to someone else.
